system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons causes mixed spasticity, weakness, fasciculations, and muscle atrophy while sensation remains relatively preserved.
vignette: A 58-year-old man has progressive hand weakness, fasciculations, muscle atrophy, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response. Sensory examination is normal.
distractor_notes: Multiple sclerosis is a CNS demyelinating disease with sensory and other disseminated CNS deficits rather than combined upper and lower motor neuron degeneration.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness without upper motor neuron signs or fasciculations.
Guillain-Barré causes acute ascending weakness and areflexia rather than chronic mixed UMN/LMN signs.
Diabetic neuropathy prominently affects sensation and causes peripheral lower motor neuron findings without upper motor neuron signs.
key_expl: The combination of upper and lower motor neuron findings with preserved sensation is classic for ALS.
objective: Recognize ALS from progressive mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.

sources.title: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)
sources.support: NINDS describes ALS as progressive degeneration of motor neurons causing weakness, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and upper motor neuron signs.

sources.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes ALS as a motor neuron disease causing progressive weakness with preserved sensation.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release; repeated activity can transiently improve strength by increasing presynaptic calcium.
vignette: A 63-year-old smoker has proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, reduced reflexes, and strength that improves briefly after repeated muscle activation.
lead: Which structure is most likely targeted by autoantibodies?
distractors: Voltage-gated sodium channels at nodes of Ranvier
distractor_notes: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, where reflexes are usually preserved and strength worsens with use.
Nodal sodium channel dysfunction would cause peripheral nerve conduction abnormalities, not facilitation with repeated activation.
Ryanodine receptor defects cause malignant hyperthermia susceptibility or congenital myopathy, not this autoimmune syndrome.
Dopamine transporter abnormalities do not cause neuromuscular junction weakness.
key_expl: Lambert-Eaton syndrome targets presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels and reduces acetylcholine release.
objective: Differentiate Lambert-Eaton from myasthenia by presynaptic calcium-channel autoimmunity and facilitation.
clues: hyporeflexia and improvement with repeated use

sources.title: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Lambert-Eaton syndrome as an autoimmune disorder affecting nerve-muscle communication, often associated with small-cell lung cancer.

sources.title: Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome
sources.support: NINDS describes antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels reducing acetylcholine release.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Spinal cord hemisection damages ipsilateral corticospinal and dorsal column tracts below the lesion while interrupting crossed spinothalamic fibers, producing contralateral pain and temperature loss.
vignette: After a stab wound to the right thoracic spinal cord, a patient has right-leg weakness and loss of vibration sense below the lesion with loss of pain and temperature on the left beginning a few segments lower.
lead: Which lesion best explains this pattern?
correct: Right hemisection of the spinal cord
distractor_notes: Complete transection would cause bilateral deficits below the lesion.
Anterior spinal artery infarction causes bilateral motor and pain-temperature loss with relative dorsal column sparing.
Bilateral dorsal column disease would impair vibration and proprioception bilaterally without this crossed motor/pain pattern.
An internal capsule lesion produces contralateral motor deficits above and below the face-body axis, not a spinal sensory level.
key_expl: Ipsilateral motor/proprioceptive loss plus contralateral pain-temperature loss below a spinal lesion is Brown-Sequard syndrome from hemisection.
objective: Localize Brown-Sequard syndrome using spinal tract crossing patterns.

sources.title: Spinal Cord Injuries
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes spinal cord injury as disrupting motor and sensory pathways below the lesion.

sources.title: Brown-Sequard Syndrome
sources.support: NINDS describes Brown-Sequard syndrome as a spinal cord lesion producing weakness or paralysis on one side of the body with sensory loss on the opposite side.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Thiamine deficiency impairs thiamine-dependent oxidative metabolism in vulnerable brain regions, producing confusion, ocular motor abnormalities, and gait ataxia.
vignette: A 50-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder has confusion, horizontal nystagmus, and a broad-based unsteady gait.
distractor_notes: Hepatic encephalopathy can cause confusion but does not classically produce the triad of ocular abnormalities and gait ataxia in a malnourished patient.
Parkinson disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor.
Multiple sclerosis is typically relapsing and multifocal in younger adults.
Normal pressure hydrocephalus causes gait impairment, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence, not nystagmus in the context of thiamine deficiency.
key_expl: Confusion, ocular motor abnormalities, and ataxia in a malnourished patient strongly indicate Wernicke encephalopathy.
objective: Recognize Wernicke encephalopathy from the classic thiamine-deficiency neurologic triad.

sources.title: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Wernicke encephalopathy as a thiamine-deficiency disorder with confusion, eye movement abnormalities, and ataxia.

sources.title: Thiamin — Health Professional Fact Sheet
sources.support: NIH ODS describes neurologic consequences of severe thiamine deficiency, including Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Rupture of an intracranial aneurysm releases arterial blood into the subarachnoid space, causing abrupt meningeal irritation and a thunderclap headache.
vignette: A 49-year-old woman develops the sudden worst headache of her life while exercising, followed by vomiting and neck stiffness.
distractor_notes: Migraine typically evolves over minutes and is recurrent rather than an abrupt maximal-at-onset thunderclap headache with meningismus.
Epidural hematoma usually follows head trauma and may have a lucid interval.
Subdural hematoma usually follows tearing of bridging veins after trauma and presents more gradually.
Temporal arteritis occurs mainly in older adults with scalp tenderness and inflammatory symptoms.
key_expl: A sudden maximal-intensity headache with vomiting and neck stiffness is classic for subarachnoid hemorrhage.
objective: Recognize aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage from a thunderclap headache and meningismus.

sources.title: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes SAH as bleeding into the subarachnoid space, often from an aneurysm, causing sudden severe headache and neck stiffness.

sources.title: Cerebral Aneurysms
sources.support: NINDS describes aneurysm rupture as causing sudden severe headache and subarachnoid hemorrhage.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Temporal bone fracture can tear the middle meningeal artery, causing arterial blood to collect between skull and dura in a lens-shaped hematoma.
vignette: A 20-year-old man is struck on the temple. He briefly loses consciousness, awakens and talks normally, then rapidly deteriorates. CT shows a biconvex extra-axial hematoma.
lead: Which vessel was most likely injured?
distractor_notes: Bridging veins are the typical source of subdural hematoma.
Anterior cerebral artery injury does not produce the classic lens-shaped epidural pattern.
Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis or injury has a different presentation.
PICA lesions produce posterior circulation ischemic syndromes, not temporal epidural hematoma.
key_expl: A temporal impact, lucid interval, and biconvex hematoma indicate epidural bleeding from the middle meningeal artery.
objective: Identify the middle meningeal artery as the typical source of traumatic epidural hematoma.
clues: temporal head trauma and lucid interval

sources.title: Epidural hematoma
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes epidural hematoma as bleeding between skull and dura, often from arterial injury after skull fracture.

sources.title: Traumatic Brain Injury
sources.support: NINDS describes traumatic intracranial hemorrhages as serious complications of head injury.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Acceleration-deceleration tears cortical bridging veins, allowing venous blood to collect between dura and arachnoid, especially in older adults with cerebral atrophy.
vignette: An 81-year-old man on anticoagulation develops gradually worsening headache and confusion several days after a minor fall. CT shows a crescent-shaped extra-axial collection crossing suture lines.
lead: Which vessels are most likely injured?
distractor_notes: Middle meningeal artery rupture causes epidural hematoma, usually biconvex.
Lenticulostriate artery rupture causes deep intraparenchymal hemorrhage.
Basilar artery disease causes posterior circulation ischemia or hemorrhage, not a crescentic subdural collection.
Retinal artery occlusion causes monocular visual loss.
key_expl: Subdural hematoma classically results from torn bridging veins and appears crescent-shaped on CT.
objective: Identify bridging-vein injury as the source of subdural hematoma.
clues: elderly anticoagulated patient after minor fall

sources.title: Subdural hematoma
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes subdural hematoma as bleeding beneath the dura, commonly from torn veins after trauma and especially in older adults.

sources.title: Traumatic Brain Injury
sources.support: NINDS describes subdural hemorrhage as a traumatic complication caused by bleeding around the brain.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Acute peripheral facial nerve dysfunction causes ipsilateral weakness of both upper and lower facial muscles because the lesion is distal to bilateral corticobulbar input to the forehead.
vignette: A 35-year-old woman develops acute left facial weakness. She cannot wrinkle the left forehead, close the left eye tightly, or smile symmetrically. Limb strength and sensation are normal.
distractor_notes: A cortical facial weakness usually spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation.
Trigeminal neuropathy affects facial sensation and mastication, not facial expression.
Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness and does not produce an isolated complete unilateral facial palsy.
Horner syndrome causes ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis rather than full facial motor paralysis.
key_expl: Weakness of the entire ipsilateral face, including forehead, localizes to a peripheral facial nerve lesion.
objective: Differentiate peripheral facial palsy from cortical facial weakness using forehead involvement.

sources.title: Bell's palsy
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Bell palsy as sudden weakness or paralysis of facial muscles on one side.

sources.title: Bell's Palsy
sources.support: NINDS describes Bell palsy as acute peripheral facial nerve weakness affecting one side of the face.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Abnormal inner-ear fluid homeostasis produces episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness.
vignette: A 46-year-old woman has recurrent 2-hour episodes of spinning vertigo with tinnitus, fullness, and fluctuating hearing loss in the left ear.
distractor_notes: BPPV causes brief positional vertigo lasting seconds and does not cause fluctuating hearing loss or tinnitus.
Vestibular neuritis causes prolonged acute vertigo without auditory symptoms.
Acoustic trauma causes hearing injury but not recurrent episodic vertigo with aural fullness.
Otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss rather than episodic vertigo and fluctuating sensorineural loss.
key_expl: Episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness is classic Meniere disease.
objective: Recognize Meniere disease from its characteristic vestibular and auditory symptom cluster.
clues: fluctuating hearing loss with tinnitus and aural fullness

sources.title: Meniere disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Meniere disease as recurrent vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, and ear pressure/fullness.

sources.title: Meniere's Disease
sources.support: NIDCD describes Meniere disease as an inner-ear disorder with episodic vertigo and fluctuating hearing symptoms.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Interruption of sympathetic innervation to the eye causes ipsilateral miosis, mild ptosis, and anhidrosis.
vignette: A patient with an apical lung mass has right-sided ptosis, miosis, and decreased facial sweating.
correct: Ipsilateral sympathetic pathway to the eye and face
distractors: Parasympathetic fibers in cranial nerve III
Somatic motor fibers in cranial nerve VI
Facial motor fibers in cranial nerve VII
distractor_notes: CN III parasympathetic injury causes mydriasis rather than miosis.
CN VI controls lateral rectus movement and does not cause anhidrosis.
CN VII controls facial expression and some autonomic functions but not the classic ptosis-miosis-anhidrosis triad.
Optic nerve lesions cause visual loss and afferent pupillary defects, not this sympathetic syndrome.
key_expl: Horner syndrome reflects disruption of the sympathetic pathway to the eye and face.
objective: Localize ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis to sympathetic pathway injury.

sources.title: Horner syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes Horner syndrome as sympathetic nerve disruption causing ptosis, miosis, and decreased sweating.

sources.title: Horner Syndrome
sources.support: NIH GARD describes Horner syndrome as a disorder of the sympathetic pathway to the eye and face.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Hemiballismus is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterized by sudden, violent, high-amplitude flinging movements affecting one side of the body and commonly reflects contralateral basal-ganglia dysfunction.
vignette: A 70-year-old woman develops sudden, irregular, large-amplitude flinging movements of the left arm and leg after a small stroke. The movements are involuntary and worsen with activity.
lead: Which movement disorder best describes these findings?
distractor_notes: Chorea consists of brief, irregular, dance-like movements that are generally less violent and lower in amplitude than the ballistic flinging described here.
Athetosis consists of slow, writhing movements rather than sudden high-amplitude flinging.
Myoclonus consists of brief shock-like jerks rather than sustained ballistic flinging of proximal limbs.
Dystonia consists of sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing patterned twisting movements or abnormal postures.
key_expl: Sudden violent, high-amplitude flinging movements affecting one side of the body are characteristic of hemiballismus.
objective: Recognize hemiballismus from unilateral violent high-amplitude flinging movements.

sources.title: Hemiballismus — NIH Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center
sources.support: NIH GARD describes hemiballismus as involuntary flinging movements of the extremities, often violent and high in amplitude, caused by dysfunction in basal-ganglia regions.

sources.title: Movement Disorders
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes movement disorders as neurologic conditions causing abnormal involuntary movements and provides the clinical context for differentiating hyperkinetic movement phenotypes.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Dominant inferior frontal cortex injury impairs language production while relatively preserving comprehension, often with contralateral face-arm weakness from nearby motor cortex involvement.
vignette: A right-handed 67-year-old man after stroke speaks slowly in short effortful phrases. He understands commands and is frustrated by his speech impairment.
lead: Which cortical region is most likely injured?
distractor_notes: Posterior superior temporal injury causes Wernicke aphasia with fluent but poorly comprehended speech.
Nondominant parietal injury causes hemispatial neglect.
Primary visual cortex lesions cause visual field defects.
Bilateral hippocampal injury causes severe anterograde memory impairment.
key_expl: Broca aphasia results from dominant inferior frontal injury and causes nonfluent effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
objective: Localize nonfluent aphasia to the dominant inferior frontal gyrus.

sources.title: Aphasia
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes aphasia as acquired language dysfunction from brain injury, including impaired speaking and understanding.

sources.title: Aphasia
sources.support: NIDCD describes Broca aphasia as nonfluent speech from frontal language-region injury with relatively preserved comprehension.
